cves.summary:
## Summary

The bash activator puts the caller-supplied prompt value into `PS1` unescaped whenever `promptvars` is off at activation time, and assumes prompt expansion can never run afterwards. `promptvars` and posix mode are runtime shell state, not a property of the activation moment: re-enabling prompt expansion in the same shell (`shopt -s promptvars`, `set -o posix`) or starting an interactive child bash that inherits the exported `PS1` makes bash expand the stored value and run the command substitution in it. An attacker who controls the prompt value gets command execution as the user who sources `bin/activate`.

This is a regression. 21.14.8 escaped `$` and the backtick unconditionally and stays inert under the same sequence. The 21.14.9 fix for GHSA-6w3r-xr62-4xcp (#3418) rewrote that block and left bash with a path that stores the raw value whenever `promptvars` is off.

## Affected area

Activation scripts (activate, activate.bat, activate.csh, activate.fish, activate.nu, Activate.ps1, activate.xsh) — specifically the bash `bin/activate`.

## Attacker-controlled input

The `--prompt` value, which the security policy already lists as a value that may come from project metadata the user did not write. It reaches `virtualenv` as `--prompt` on the command line or as the `prompt` argument of the API, is written into `bin/activate` as the literal `VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT` assignment (correctly quoted, the value arrives there as data), and the script then copies it into `PS1` without escaping `$` or the backtick.

Example: a repository or tool config supplies a prompt such as `x$(id > /tmp/ve-pwn)y`; the victim creates and later activates the environment.

## Details

Source of the latest release: [`src/virtualenv/activation/bash/activate.sh` lines 140-160](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/21.14.12/src/virtualenv/activation/bash/activate.sh#L140-L160)

```sh
if [ -z "${VIRTUAL_ENV_DISABLE_PROMPT-}" ] &&
    { [ -n "${BASH_VERSION-}" ] || [ -n "${ZSH_VERSION-}" ]; }; then
    _OLD_VIRTUAL_PS1="${PS1-}"
    # bash expands PS1 after decoding its prompt escapes when promptvars is on or in posix mode, so the prompt holds a
    # reference to the variable and its value never reaches that expansion; otherwise only the decode runs and
    # backslashes need doubling. ...
    if [ -n "${BASH_VERSION-}" ] && { shopt -q promptvars || shopt -qo posix; }; then
        PS1='(${VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT-}) '"${PS1-}"
    else
        _VIRTUAL_PROMPT="${VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT//\\/\\\\}"
        if [ -n "${ZSH_VERSION-}" ]; then
            _VIRTUAL_PROMPT="${_VIRTUAL_PROMPT//\$/\\\$}"
            _VIRTUAL_PROMPT="${_VIRTUAL_PROMPT//\`/\\\`}"
            _VIRTUAL_PROMPT="${_VIRTUAL_PROMPT//\%/%%}"
        fi
        PS1="(${_VIRTUAL_PROMPT}) ${PS1-}"
        unset _VIRTUAL_PROMPT
    fi
fi
```

Two separate mistakes combine:

1. A runtime shell option is treated as a constant. `shopt -u promptvars` at the moment of `source` does not bind the shell forever: `shopt -s promptvars` and `set -o posix` both re-enable PS1 expansion in the same shell. The code itself tests `shopt -qo posix` because posix mode expands the prompt regardless of `promptvars`, which shows the expansion state is not fixed by the activation.
2. The escaping that would keep the value inert in that mode is missing for bash. GHSA-5vjq-rrrf-7h2q ("activate runs commands from the environment name in zsh with PROMPT_SUBST") fixed exactly this shape for zsh, reasoning that "a user can set it after activation", by escaping `$` and the backtick. Bash lost the equivalent escaping in the same commit that added the zsh branch.

The rendered prompt shows the regression directly:

```
21.14.8   PS1 = (x\\$(id > /tmp/ve-pwn)y)       <- escaped, inert
21.14.9   PS1 = (x$(id > /tmp/ve-pwn)y)         <- raw value
21.14.12  PS1 = (x$(id > /tmp/ve-pwn)y)         <- raw value
```

Relevant commit: [`5f48d711` "fix(bash): preserve literal prompts in supported shells (#3418)"](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/commit/5f48d711731311428aebfae61d46957762155b22), which removed the unconditional `$`/backtick escaping from the bash path. Advisory for that change: [GHSA-6w3r-xr62-4xcp](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/security/advisories/GHSA-6w3r-xr62-4xcp).

## Proof of concept

Non-destructive payload: it runs `id` and writes the output to a file.

```bash
python -m virtualenv --no-seed --no-periodic-update --activators bash \
    --prompt 'x$(id > /tmp/ve-pwn)y' /tmp/venv-demo

cat > /tmp/rc <<'EOF'
shopt -u promptvars
. /tmp/venv-demo/bin/activate
shopt -s promptvars
EOF

# the prompt needs a tty; script(1) provides one
printf 'exit\n' | script -qec 'bash --noprofile --rcfile /tmp/rc -i' /dev/null

cat /tmp/ve-pwn
```

Observed on 21.14.12:

```
$ cat /tmp/ve-pwn
uid=1000(asrun) gid=1000(asrun) groups=1000(asrun),4(adm),24(cdrom),27(sudo),30(dip),46(plugdev),999(ollama)
```

The prompt printed as `(xy)`. The same script against 21.14.8 creates no file; against 21.14.9 and 21.14.12 it does.

Triggers, all run in a pty, activation itself never executing anything; execution happens at the next prompt redraw after prompt expansion is enabled:

| After `. bin/activate` (activated with `shopt -u promptvars`) | 21.14.8 | 21.14.9 | 21.14.12 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `shopt -s promptvars` | inert | executes | executes |
| `set -o posix` | inert | executes | executes |
| `export PS1`, then start an interactive child `bash` (its `promptvars` defaults to on) | inert | executes | executes |
| control: activation with default options | inert | inert | inert |
| control: activation with `set -o posix` already on | inert | inert | inert |

The third trigger needs no explicit option change: the poisoned `PS1` is inherited and the child bash expands it on its first prompt.

`shopt -u promptvars` is a documented way to make an expensive bash prompt cheap and appears in `~/.bashrc` files for that reason; it is also the state left by some prompt wrappers. Whoever sources such an environment gets the unescaped value in `PS1`.

## Impact

Command execution as the user who sources `bin/activate`, from a value the user may not have written (project metadata or tool config reaching `--prompt`). The value is also persisted in `pyvenv.cfg` and in the generated script, so it survives the activation that created it and fires later, in a different shell session, on the first prompt redraw with expansion enabled. No privilege elevation beyond the activating user.

Severity: high, matching GHSA-5vjq-rrrf-7h2q for the same class of prompt-expansion command injection reached by toggling a shell option after activation. If you consider the `promptvars` state a caller-controlled condition rather than a shell condition, this is medium; the fix is the same either way.

## Versions tested

virtualenv 21.14.12 and 21.14.9 (affected), virtualenv 21.14.8 (unaffected control); CPython 3.14.7; Linux 6.x (WSL2); bash 5.1.16(1)-release. `--prompt` handling is platform independent; zsh/fish/csh/nu/PowerShell activators were not part of this report.

## Known mitigation

For a user: activate with `promptvars` left at its default, or set `VIRTUAL_ENV_DISABLE_PROMPT=1` before activating, which skips the whole prompt block. Do not pass an untrusted value to `--prompt`.

Fix in the activator: escape `$` and the backtick for bash as well, in both branches, with a single backslash (`$` -> `\$`, backtick -> ``\` ``, `\` -> `\\`). Verified on bash 5.1.16 that a `PS1` built that way is inert with `promptvars` on, with `promptvars` off, and with `promptvars` off followed by posix mode, while still rendering the literal value on screen. That is better than both current shapes: 21.14.8's four-level escaping left stray backslashes on screen, which is why the block was rewritten.

```sh
    else
        _VIRTUAL_PROMPT="${VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT//\\/\\\\}"
        _VIRTUAL_PROMPT="${_VIRTUAL_PROMPT//\$/\\\$}"
        _VIRTUAL_PROMPT="${_VIRTUAL_PROMPT//\`/\\\`}"
        if [ -n "${ZSH_VERSION-}" ]; then
            _VIRTUAL_PROMPT="${_VIRTUAL_PROMPT//\%/%%}"
        fi
        PS1="(${_VIRTUAL_PROMPT}) ${PS1-}"
```

For the tests, `tests/unit/activation/test_bash.py::test_bash_prompt_options` already parametrises `("before", "after", "expected")` and covers `before="shopt -u promptvars"` with `after=""`. The missing axis is the transition: `("shopt -u promptvars", "shopt -s promptvars", ...)` and `("shopt -u promptvars", "set -o posix", ...)`, with the existing `PWNED` check asserting no file was created.

## Latest release

- [x] The problem reproduces on the latest virtualenv release.

cwe.name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')

cves.summary:
The Include directive in `src/mistune/directives/include.py` does not validate that the resolved file path stays within the source directory, allowing path traversal via `../` sequences to read arbitrary files.

Additionally, error messages and included file contents are rendered without HTML escaping, leading to XSS even when `escape=True`.

Affected functions:
- Path resolution (lines 27-31)
- `block_error()` in html.py (line 140)
- `render_html_include()` (line 72)

The Include plugin must be explicitly enabled via the plugins parameter.

cwe.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

cves.summary:
## Summary

An infinite-loop vulnerability (CWE-835) in the Twisted IMAP4 server lets an authenticated client freeze the whole process with one small command. `twisted.mail.imap4.parseNestedParens` reads an IMAP literal size with `int()` and never rejects a negative value. A negative size such as `{-100}` drives the parser cursor negative, and because a negative Python index wraps around the end of the string instead of raising, the scanning loop never terminates. It runs synchronously on the single-threaded reactor, so one `SEARCH` command holds the reactor at full CPU forever and every other connection stops being served.

## Details

Meeting an inline literal, `parseNestedParens` reads the size between the braces and advances the cursor past the body:

```python
# twisted/mail/imap4.py  parseNestedParens
literalSize = int(s[i + 1 : end])          # no sign check
contentStack[-1].append((s[end + 3 : end + 3 + literalSize],))
i = end + 3 + literalSize                    # negative size -> i goes negative
```

`int(b"-100")` is `-100`, so `i` goes negative; the loop condition `i < len(s)` stays true and `s[i : i + 1]` on a negative index never raises, so the cursor cycles forever. The `_literalStringLimit` guard only covers the synchronizing-literal continuation path, not this inline branch. The call is reached from `select_SEARCH` through `arg_searchkeys`, dispatched only in the selected state, so a valid login and a selected mailbox (any low-privilege account) suffice. It runs in the reactor thread, and the connection timeout cannot fire because the reactor itself is frozen.

Affected product: Twisted (`twisted.mail`), the IMAP4 server `twisted.mail.imap4.IMAP4Server`
Affected versions: 26.4.0 and earlier

## PoC

Log in, select a mailbox, and send a `SEARCH` whose literal size is negative:

```text
C: t1 LOGIN testuser password-test
C: t2 SELECT INBOX
C: t3 SEARCH {-100}zzzzzzzzzz
```

The server never responds and one core stays at 100 percent. In a measured run a health service co-hosted on the same reactor stopped answering the instant the command arrived, showing the freeze hits the whole process and not just the attacking connection. A valid `{5}zzzzz` completes normally and a non-numeric `{abc}` is rejected with a parse error, which isolates the cause to the missing negative-size check.

## Impact

A remote denial of service. One command of about ten bytes freezes the single-threaded reactor, so it stops serving not only every other IMAP connection but every other service co-hosted in the same process (for example SMTP and POP3 under `twistd mail`), and no timeout can recover it until the process is restarted. It requires an authenticated session, so any account holder can trigger it; there is no confidentiality or integrity impact and no code execution.

## Summary

An unbounded-buffer vulnerability (CWE-770) in the Twisted words IRC server lets any unauthenticated remote client exhaust server memory. `twisted.words.protocols.irc.IRC.dataReceived` appends every received byte to a per-connection buffer and only removes data at a line feed, with no maximum length. Because `IRC` is a plain `Protocol` and not a `LineReceiver`, one connection that streams bytes without a line feed grows the buffer without bound and drives the whole single-threaded process to out-of-memory, dropping every user at once. The `twistd words` server inherits the method unchanged through `IRCUser`, and the data is buffered before any authentication.

## Details

`IRC.dataReceived` keeps everything up to the last line feed in `self.buffer`:

```python
# twisted/words/protocols/irc.py
class IRC(protocol.Protocol):        # not a LineReceiver, so no MAX_LENGTH
    buffer = ""
    def dataReceived(self, data):
        if isinstance(data, bytes):
            data = data.decode("utf-8")
        lines = (self.buffer + data).split(LF)
        self.buffer = lines.pop()    # no 3line feed -> whole input stays buffered
        ...
```

With no line feed in the data, `lines.pop()` returns the entire accumulated content to `self.buffer`, so it grows by every chunk and is never bounded; `IRC` defines no `MAX_LENGTH`, no `lineLengthExceeded`, and no timeout, so the connection is never closed. The `twistd words` server protocol `IRCUser` subclasses `IRC` without overriding `dataReceived`, and the buffer is filled before any `PASS`, `NICK`, or `USER`, so no credentials are required.

Affected product: Twisted (`twisted.words`), `twisted.words.protocols.irc.IRC` and its subclass `twisted.words.service.IRCUser`
Affected versions: 26.4.0 and earlier

## PoC

On a standard Twisted words IRC server (the server `twistd words` runs, using `IRCUser`), an unauthenticated client opens a single TCP connection and continuously sends data that contains no line feed, never completing a line. Every chunk is appended to the connection's line buffer, and because no complete line is ever formed none of it is consumed, so the buffer grows by the full volume sent.

In a measured run against a real `IRCFactory` server, one unauthenticated connection sending 60 MB of line-feed-free data raised the server process resident memory from about 47 MB to 2966 MB (roughly 49 MB per MB sent) with the connection still open and no limit triggered. Sending the same volume as normal line-feed-terminated commands leaves memory flat, which isolates the cause to the missing line-length bound.

## Impact

An unauthenticated remote denial of service from allocation without limits (CWE-770) leading to uncontrolled resource consumption (CWE-400). A single credential-free connection exhausts the memory of the whole `twistd words` process, and because one process serves every user, the crash drops all connections at once and the service stays down until it is restarted. The quadratic buffer copy reaches the same effect faster. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact and no code execution.

## Summary

An allocation-without-limits vulnerability (CWE-770) in the Twisted conch telnet transport lets any unauthenticated remote peer exhaust server memory over a single connection. When the peer opens a telnet subnegotiation with `IAC SB` and then streams bytes without ever sending the `IAC SE` terminator, every byte is appended to a per-connection buffer that has no maximum length. The buffer persists across reads and is released only on the terminator the attacker withholds, so it grows without bound until the process is killed.

## Details

The option-negotiation state machine in `Telnet.dataReceived` enters the `subnegotiation` state on `IAC SB` and sets an empty command list. In that state every non-`IAC` byte is appended to the list with no length check:

```python
# src/twisted/conch/telnet.py  (Telnet.dataReceived)
elif self.state == "subnegotiation":
    if b == IAC:
        self.state = "subnegotiation-escaped"
    else:
        self.commands.append(b)      # unbounded: no len(self.commands) check
```

`self.commands` is an instance attribute that persists across `dataReceived` calls and is deleted only when `IAC SE` completes the subnegotiation. Negotiation runs at the transport layer before authentication, and the bytes are consumed inside `dataReceived` before any application callback, so an application cannot impose a bound. Twisted caps other parser buffers, for example `NetstringReceiver.MAX_LENGTH`, but not this one.

Affected product: Twisted, `twisted.conch.telnet` transport
Affected versions: confirmed against 26.4.0

## PoC

On any endpoint that exposes the Twisted telnet transport, such as the Twisted manhole telnet service, open one connection and send the two bytes `IAC SB` (`0xFF 0xFA`), then stream any non-`0xFF` bytes continuously and never send the `IAC SE` terminator (`0xFF 0xF0`). No credentials are required, because option negotiation runs before authentication.

Every byte is appended to the per-connection subnegotiation buffer with no maximum, and the buffer is released only by the terminator the attacker withholds, so it grows for the life of the connection. Because each byte is retained as a separate element the memory consumed is several times the traffic sent, so a modest-bandwidth peer, or several such connections, drives the process to memory exhaustion.

## Impact

This is an unauthenticated remote denial of service (CWE-770, CWE-400) by memory exhaustion. A single connection grows an in-memory buffer without bound at a cost proportional to the bytes sent, amplified by per-byte object overhead, until the operating system kills the server and every service it hosts. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact and no code execution. The affected surface is any deployment that exposes a Twisted telnet or manhole transport to untrusted peers.

## Summary

An allocation-without-limits vulnerability in the Twisted XML element stream lets any unauthenticated remote peer exhaust server memory over a single stream. When the peer opens a container element and streams child elements without ever closing the container, every element is materialised into an in-memory tree with no limit on depth or child count. An element is released only when its end tag arrives, so a container the attacker never closes retains everything beneath it until the process is killed.

## Details

In `ExpatElementStream._onStartElement`, each start tag appends a new element to the current element's children and descends into it, with no depth or child-count check:

```python
# src/twisted/words/xish/domish.py  (ExpatElementStream._onStartElement)
if self.documentStarted == 1:
    if self.currElem != None:
        self.currElem.children.append(e)   # append child: no depth/count cap
        e.parent = self.currElem
    self.currElem = e                      # descend into the new element
```

An element is emitted and dropped only when its end tag arrives while it sits directly under the document root, so a container that is never closed keeps every child beneath it. The transport `XmlStream.dataReceived` feeds bytes to `self.stream.parse(data)` with no size limit, and in XMPP the stream is parsed during negotiation before authentication.

Affected product: Twisted, `twisted.words.xish.domish` element stream
Affected versions: confirmed against 26.4.0

## PoC

On any endpoint that parses untrusted XML streams with this stack, such as an XMPP server, open a stream by sending the opening `stream:stream` tag and a container element, then stream child elements continuously and never send the container's closing tag. No credentials are required, because in XMPP the stream is parsed before authentication.

Every child is appended to the container and retained because the container is never emitted, and the transport applies no limit on the size of the unfinished document. Because each small element becomes a full object in memory the footprint is many times the traffic sent, so a modest-bandwidth peer, or several such streams, drives the process to memory exhaustion.

## Impact

This is an unauthenticated remote denial of service by memory exhaustion. A single stream grows an in-memory element tree without bound, amplified by per-element object overhead, until the operating system kills the server. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact and no code execution. The affected surface is any deployment that parses untrusted XML streams with this stack, such as an XMPP server or component.

## Summary

An incomplete header-value validation (CWE-444) in the Twisted HTTP server lets a bare carriage return or line feed in a header value hide a following header from the parser. `twisted.web.http.HTTPChannel.headerReceived` rejects a NUL byte in a header value but not a bare CR or LF, even though RFC 9110 section 5.5 requires a recipient to reject all three. Because the channel splits requests only on CRLF, a value carrying a bare LF and a second header arrives as one line, so the second header is folded into the value and the request is framed with no body. A front-end that treats the bare LF as a line terminator frames the request differently, and the disagreement lets an attacker smuggle a request past it. This is an incomplete fix of the earlier Twisted request-smuggling advisories, which guarded the NUL sibling of this exact check.

## Details

`headerReceived` splits a header line on the first colon, strips space and tab from the value, and validates it with a single test that rejects only NUL:

```python
# twisted/web/http.py  HTTPChannel.headerReceived
data = data.strip(b" \t")
if b"\x00" in data:          # NUL rejected; a bare CR or LF is not
    self._respondToBadRequestAndDisconnect()
    return False
```

The channel delimiter is CRLF, so `Foo: x\nContent-Length: 39` is one line: the split yields name `Foo` and value `x\nContent-Length: 39`, `strip` leaves the LF, and the NUL check passes. `_maybeChooseTransferDecoder` is then called with `Foo`, never sees a `Content-Length`, and installs no body decoder, so the request is framed with an empty body. The header name and request line already reject CR and LF, so the value is the only gap.

Affected product: Twisted, `twisted.web.http.HTTPChannel`
Affected versions: 26.4.0 and earlier

## PoC

Feed one connection a request whose header value carries a bare LF and a `Content-Length`, followed by a second request in the bytes after it: `POST /public HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: v\r\nFoo: x\nContent-Length: 44\r\n\r\nGET /admin HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: internal\r\n\r\n`. Twisted parses two requests and serves both, so the smuggled `GET /admin` returns the /admin response body even though the visible request was only `POST /public`. The bare CR variant behaves identically, and a NUL in the value is rejected, which isolates the missing CR and LF checks.

Behind a front-end that treats the bare LF as a line terminator, the front-end frames one `POST /public` and forwards a body while Twisted frames a second `GET /admin`; the extra response then poisons the shared connection, so a later victim receives the attacker's `GET /admin` response.

## Impact

This is an HTTP request-smuggling exposure (CWE-444) from inconsistent interpretation of a request (CWE-436). Through a front-end that accepts a bare CR or LF as a line terminator, an attacker can smuggle a request the front-end never sees, bypassing front-end access controls, poisoning a shared connection so a later victim receives the attacker's response, and poisoning a cache. Twisted is the strict endpoint that frames the request without a body, so it is realized only behind such a proxy, and there is no code execution.

cwe.name: Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests ('HTTP Request/Response Smuggling')

cves.summary:
## Summary

Multimodal content parts (`image_url`, `video_url`, `input_audio`, ...) accept a user-supplied `uuid` field that vLLM uses **verbatim as the item's cache identity** (`mm_hash`). The two frontend/engine processor caches (P0 "sender" cache in the API process, P1 "receiver" cache in the EngineCore process) are independent LRU caches whose evictions are **not synchronized**, and the P1 hit path performs **zero consistency validation** — it silently substitutes the cached item's tensor data for whatever the current request actually contains.

A single unauthenticated client can exploit this to kill the entire engine, deterministically, with default server flags:

1. **Seed**: send a small image with `uuid="U"`. Both caches now map `U` to an item with **N_A** visual tokens (e.g. 4).
2. **Drift**: send ~70 requests, each carrying a *unique* uuid, a max-size image, and an over-long text prompt. Each request is rejected with 400 — but **after** its image has been inserted into the P0 cache (insertion happens during chat rendering, before prompt-length validation), so these requests fill P0 **without ever reaching the engine/P1**. `U` is evicted from P0 only.
3. **Kill**: send a *large* image with `uuid="U"`. P0 misses → the image is freshly processed and the prompt is spliced with **N_B** (e.g. 2048+) placeholder tokens; the request carries full data to the engine, but P1 still has `U` → the engine **discards the fresh data and substitutes the stale N_A-row tensor**. The scheduler plans for N_B encoder slots while the worker merges N_A embeddings into N_B placeholders → `ValueError: Attempted to assign 4 = 4 multimodal tokens to 2048 placeholders` at `vllm/model_executor/models/utils.py:711` → uncaught in the EngineCore busy loop → `_send_engine_dead()` → the EngineCore process dies, every API server reports `EngineDeadError` and shuts down. `/health` never recovers; the deployment needs a full restart.

Verified end-to-end on the official `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.29.0` image with Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct, default configuration (no flags beyond `--served-model-name`/`--gpu-memory-utilization`): after 70 flood requests the kill request returned `500 EngineCore encountered an issue` and `/health` went dead permanently. The vulnerable code is byte-identical on `main` (post-0.29.0).

## Details

**1. The client-controlled `uuid` becomes the cache hash verbatim.** `vllm/entrypoints/chat_utils.py:1677` / `:1884-1886` read `part["uuid"]` per content part and pass it through as `mm_uuids`. In `vllm/multimodal/processing/inputs.py:62-63`, when no `hf_processor_mm_kwargs` are present (the default for chat requests), the uuid string **is** the item hash — no content binding at all:

```python
# vllm/multimodal/processing/inputs.py:62-63
else:
    hashes.append(uuid_item)        # client string used verbatim as mm_hash
```

**2. P0 insertion happens before request validation.** In the serving path, `render_chat_request` (`vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/serving.py:275`) runs full mm processing — `mm_processor.apply` (`vllm/renderers/base.py:759`) → `_cached_apply_hf_processor` → `_merge_mm_kwargs` → `cache.get_and_update_item` (`vllm/multimodal/processing/processor.py:1338`), which inserts the processed item into the P0 sender cache (default `mm_processor_cache_type="lru"`, 4 GiB). Only afterwards does `get_max_tokens` (`vllm/entrypoints/serve/utils/api_utils.py:183-186`) reject over-long prompts with 400. **A request can therefore write to P0 while never reaching the engine** — the primitive that desynchronizes P0 from P1. (Public issue #43941 documented this same asymmetry for the opposite drift direction, which was later handled via `MultiModalCacheMissError`; the P0-miss/P1-hit direction below was never addressed.)

**3. P1 substitutes cached data on hash hit with no consistency check.** In the EngineCore input thread, `preprocess_add_request` (`vllm/v1/engine/core.py:997-1000`) calls `mm_receiver_cache.get_and_update_features`, which only replaces `feature.data` (`vllm/multimodal/cache.py:673-690`) and keeps the request's own `mm_position` (placeholder layout). On a cache hit the receiver cache returns the stale item wholesale:

```python
# vllm/multimodal/cache.py:739-740  (MultiModalReceiverCache.get_and_update_item)
if (cached_item := self._cache.get(mm_hash)) is not None:
    return cached_item              # fresh data silently discarded; no size/modality check
```

Only the opposite drift (P0 hit / P1 miss, `data=None`) is handled, via the retryable `MultiModalCacheMissError`. Nothing validates that the cached item's modality, shape, or token count matches the current request's placeholders.

**4. The mismatch is fatal to the engine.** The scheduler plans encoder work from the request's (fresh) placeholder count N_B, while the worker gathers embeddings from the stale N_A-row tensor (encoder-cache hit under the same forged hash, or re-encoding the stale data — both yield N_A rows). `_merge_multimodal_embeddings` then raises:

```python
# vllm/model_executor/models/utils.py:703-714
inputs_embeds[is_multimodal] = mm_embeds_flat.to(dtype=input_dtype)   # RuntimeError
...
raise ValueError(
    f"Attempted to assign {expr} = {num_actual_tokens} "
    f"multimodal tokens to {num_expected_tokens} placeholders") from e
```

This exception is raised inside the worker's input preparation with no per-request containment, propagates to the EngineCore busy loop's top-level handler (`vllm/v1/engine/core.py:1372`), and triggers `_send_engine_dead()`. The API server's `output_handler` receives `EngineDeadError` (`vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py:819`) and the whole process tree shuts down. (Issue #55546 independently reported this sink — "one bad multimodal item kills the entire V1 engine tree" — from an organically occurring stale cache entry; this report provides the missing deterministic, remote, single-attacker trigger.)

**Cost of the attack.** With the default `mm_processor_cache_gb=4`, one max-size Qwen2.5-VL image (12845056 pixels) caches as ~77 MB, so ~56 flood requests suffice; we used 70. Flood requests are CPU-only image decodes (~0.3 s each here) and can be issued sequentially or concurrently; the total wall-clock cost of the kill was under one minute. Models with larger `max_pixels` fill the cache in even fewer requests. Note that issuing the flood with *successful* requests does not work — they would populate P1 as well; rejection after P0 insertion is essential, and the over-long-prompt 400 is one always-available way to get it (no size limits depend on non-default flags).

## Impact

Any unauthenticated client that can reach a multimodal vLLM endpoint (`/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, etc. — all accept content-part `uuid`) can **deterministically crash the entire serving instance**: the EngineCore process dies, every in-flight request fails, and the API server exits; the deployment stays down until restarted. In data-parallel or multi-API-server deployments the blast radius extends to the whole engine group (cf. the DP8 outage in #55546). The attack requires no special privileges, no non-default server flags, no race conditions, and costs under a minute of sequential requests at default cache sizes.

This is distinct from the documented "Multimodal Media UUID Security" guidance in `docs/usage/security.md`, which covers only **integrity/confidentiality** consequences of uuid collisions (a caller silently receiving another caller's media). The guidance does not mention availability, and following it does not help: the attacker here deliberately collides with *their own* uuid, and the fatal element is the missing consistency check on the P1 hit path plus the unsynchronized eviction of the two caches.

**Suggested remediation** (any one of these breaks the kill chain):

1. On a P1 receiver-cache hit, validate the cached item against the request's `mm_position` (modality and expected embedding count); on mismatch, treat it as a miss (`MultiModalCacheMissError`) or reject the request — never substitute silently.
2. Make the feature/placeholder count mismatch in `_merge_multimodal_embeddings` a per-request error instead of a fatal engine exception (also requested by #55546).
3. Bind server-side cache identity to content even when a uuid is provided (e.g. `hash(content) + uuid`), eliminating forged-hash cache hits entirely.
4. Synchronize P0/P1 evictions (the engine already pushes `invalidate` to P0 on cache-miss; eviction-direction sync would close the remaining drift).

A public fix is available here: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57833

### Impact

Applications that prerender pages and use `setHeaders` to set a `cache-control` header from an untrusted source are vulnerable to cross-site scripting (XSS).

SvelteKit inserts the header value into a `<meta http-equiv="cache-control">` tag without escaping it. An attacker who can influence this value at prerender time can break out of the `content` attribute and inject HTML or JavaScript into the generated page. The injected code can then execute when users visit the page.

### Patches

The fix escapes the header value before inserting it into the generated HTML. Upgrade to `@sveltejs/kit` version 3.0.0 or later.

### Workarounds

Avoid forwarding untrusted `cache-control` header values with `setHeaders` on prerendered pages. Use a fixed, trusted cache policy instead.

### Summary
`create_entity`, `link_entities`, `rename_entity`, `unlink_entities` and `delete_entity` regenerate a memory note's body from SQLite at the computed `memory/<type>/<name>.md` path. When a note already existed at that path and was not owned by the entity being written (a hand-authored note, or an orphan left by a different entity whose name sanitized to the same path), its entire body was overwritten on the next write naming that `(type, name)`, keeping only its frontmatter. Separately, several of these tools inserted or removed their SQLite row before the fallible filesystem step, so a refused note write could leave a relation gone, a retired status committed, or the wrong entity deleted.

### Details
- `create_entity` and `link_entities` inserted the SQL row or relation before materialization.
- `rename_entity` seeded the destination path with a direct atomic write that bypassed the ownership check, and for a status-only rename could commit a retired status with the note write refused.
- `unlink_entities` removed the relation row before discovering the source note's rematerialization would be refused.
- `delete_entity`'s cascade could delete the target and its relations before a neighbour's note was found to be foreign.

The overwrite exists in every released version since `materializeEntity` shipped (`git show v1.0.1:packages/server/src/memory/materialize.ts`).

### Impact
An authorized caller with memory-write scope (any agent using the M5 memory tools) can, without intending to, destroy the body of a vault note outside the entity it is writing, and can leave the memory graph inconsistent with the notes on disk. Snapshots-before-write (`restore_note`) mitigate the overwrite only where snapshots are enabled and the note had been written through obsidian-tc before.

### Patches
Fixed in 1.31.4 at the shared primitive: `materializeEntity` refuses to write over a note whose `obsidian_tc_id` is missing or belongs to another entity; a new `assertNoteOwnership` pre-check runs before any SQLite mutation in the three lifecycle tools, so a refusal is a no-op; `create_entity` and `link_entities` roll back the row they had inserted. Verified by `test/m5-memory-ownership.test.ts`, which covers all five call sites and the rollback.

### Workarounds
None that preserve the tools. Disabling the `write:memory` scope for callers prevents the write path entirely.

### Credit
Found by the maintainer while building `obsidian-tc memory import` (PR #978); the vulnerability class was independently confirmed by a cross-vendor adversarial review.

### References
- PR #978 (fix and test), CHANGELOG `## [1.31.4] ### Security`
- `packages/server/src/memory/materialize.ts`, `packages/server/src/tools/m5/memory-lifecycle-tools.ts`

## Summary

`installBazaarPlugin` (and the equivalent endpoints for widgets/icons/templates/themes) accept
`packageName`, `repoURL`, and `repoHash` as independent request fields with no validation that
they refer to the same package. `packageName` alone determines the install destination;
`repoURL`/`repoHash` alone determine what content gets downloaded and written there. A request
can name an already-installed, already-enabled plugin as `packageName` while pointing `repoURL`/
`repoHash` at different, attacker-influenced content, silently overwriting the existing plugin's
files.

## Affected code

`kernel/api/bazaar.go`:
```go
util.BindJsonArg("packageName", &packageName, true, true)
util.BindJsonArg("repoURL", &repoURL, true, true)
util.BindJsonArg("repoHash", &repoHash, true, true)
err := model.InstallBazaarPackage("plugins", repoURL, repoHash, packageName, 0)
```

`kernel/model/bazaar.go`:
```go
func getPackageInstallPath(pkgType, packageName string) (string, string, error) {
    case "plugins":
        return filepath.Join(util.DataDir, "plugins", packageName), "plugin.json", nil
```

`kernel/bazaar/install.go`:
```go
func installPackage(data []byte, installPath string) (err error) {
    ...
    if err = filelock.Copy(srcPath, installPath); err != nil { return }
    return
}
```

`installPath` is derived solely from `packageName`; the downloaded `data` is derived solely from
`repoURL`/`repoHash`; nothing cross-validates them, and `installPackage` performs no check for
whether `installPath` already contains an existing package before copying into it. The same
pattern applies to the widget/icon/template/theme install endpoints, which share
`getPackageInstallPath`.

This does not involve path traversal — `installPath` always resolves inside
`DataDir/plugins/` (or the corresponding directory for other package types), so this is not an
instance of "arbitrary file write outside the workspace path" (excluded by this project's
SECURITY.md). The issue is that the write lands in the *wrong, existing* location within the
intended directory, not outside it — an authorization/identity-verification gap, not a path
traversal.

## Reachability / why this is not trivially remote

The bazaar endpoints are gated by `model.CheckAuth`, `model.CheckAdminRole`, `model.CheckReadonly`.
When no lock-screen password is configured (the common desktop default), `CheckAuth` still
enforces a same-origin check:
```go
if !localhost || ... || ("" != origin && !util.IsLocalOrigin(origin)) || ... {
    // reject with 401
}
```
I verified `IsLocalOrigin`/`IsLocalHostname` correctly parse the `Origin` header via `url.Parse`
and check exact hostname / loopback IP:
```go
func IsLocalOrigin(origin string) bool {
    if u, err := url.Parse(origin); err == nil {
        return IsLocalHostname(u.Hostname())
    }
    return false
}
func IsLocalHostname(hostname string) bool {
    if "localhost" == hostname || strings.HasSuffix(hostname, ".localhost") {
        return true
    }
    if ip := net.ParseIP(hostname); nil != ip {
        return ip.IsLoopback()
    }
    return false
}
```
This was tested against common bypass patterns (subdomain-suffix tricks like
`localhost.attacker.com`, and `Origin: null` as sent by sandboxed iframes) and found no bypass —
this is a correctly-implemented check. This means a purely remote attacker (e.g. a malicious
website) cannot invoke this endpoint via CSRF; a request must originate from SiYuan's own
renderer origin.

## Realistic impact

Given SiYuan runs as an Electron app with `nodeIntegration: true` (per prior advisories in this
repository), a same-origin script-execution primitive (e.g. an XSS bug in the renderer, of which
several have been fixed in this repository recently) is typically already sufficient for direct
code execution. This bug's marginal value is **persistence**: a transient XSS-driven compromise
can use this endpoint to overwrite an existing, trusted, already-enabled plugin's `index.js`,
converting a one-time compromise into code that runs on every future launch of the application,
surviving after the original XSS vector is closed.

The overwrite does not effect immediately, via this specific
endpoint. `PushReloadPlugin` (the websocket event that triggers frontend hot-reload without
restart) is only called from the batch-update path (`InstallBazaarPackages`, used by
`batchUpdatePackage`), which explicitly checks `if petal != nil && petal.Enabled` before forcing
a reload via `SetPetalEnabled`. The single-package install endpoint (`installBazaarPlugin`) does
not call `PushReloadPlugin` at all — it only pushes a generic success toast. So an overwrite via
this endpoint activates on the next app restart or manual plugin toggle, rather than instantly 
still a realistic and frequent event for a desktop application, but not an instant hot-reload.

## Suggested fix

Verify that `packageName` matches the package name declared in the downloaded package's own
`plugin.json`/`theme.json`/etc. before copying into `installPath`, and/or refuse to install over
an existing, non-empty destination directory unless the request is explicitly an update of that
same package (matching by source repo identity, not just by request-supplied name).

## Verification notes

Confirmed via static source review of `kernel/api/bazaar.go`, `kernel/model/bazaar.go`,
`kernel/bazaar/install.go`, `kernel/model/session.go` (CheckAuth), `kernel/util/net.go`
(IsLocalOrigin/IsLocalHostname), and `kernel/model/push_reload.go` /
`app/src/plugin/loader.ts` (reload trigger wiring). I do not have a running SiYuan instance
in this environment to execute an end-to-end proof of concept; findings are based on tracing
the actual, unmodified control flow across these files rather than assumption.

### Summary

Two checks on the same WebSocket request URI parse it differently. The authentication exemption for keepalive sessions matches raw substrings, while the quarantine introduced to contain those sessions reads a parsed query parameter. Because Go's `url.Values.Get` returns only the first value for a repeated key, a single URI can satisfy the exemption and still resolve to a non-auth session identity.

The result is that an unauthenticated remote caller connects to the kernel WebSocket with a valid access auth code configured, is placed in the general broadcast pool rather than the quarantined pool, and receives the live event stream.

### Details

**The exemption matches substrings.** `kernel/server/serve.go:1222` on the development branch, `:1074` on master:

```go
authOk = strings.Contains(s.Request.RequestURI, "/ws?app=siyuan") &&
         strings.Contains(s.Request.RequestURI, "&id=auth&type=auth")
```

Neither operand is parsed. Any URI containing both literals is exempted, regardless of what the query actually resolves to.

**The quarantine parses.** Commit `1e370e373` added the containment for exempted sessions at `kernel/util/websocket.go:171`:

```go
id = session.Request.URL.Query().Get("id")
return "auth" == id
```

`url.Values.Get` returns the first value for a repeated key.

**The differential.** For the URI:

```
/ws?app=siyuan&id=main&type=main&id=auth&type=auth
```

- It contains `/ws?app=siyuan` and `&id=auth&type=auth`, so `authOk` is true. No cookie, no JWT and no access auth code are required.
- `Query().Get("id")` returns `main`, so `IsAuthSession` is false. `AddPushChan` files the session in `sessions`, the broadcast pool, rather than in `authSessions`.
- `Query().Get("type")` returns `main`, so the session matches `BroadcastByType("main", ...)`.
- Without a valid `X-Auth-Token` the publish flag is never set, so `isPublishSession()` does not exclude it either.

Every guard that should have caught the session keys off a different parse than the one that admitted it.

**No origin validation.** `CheckOrigin` does not appear on the `/ws` path, so the cross-origin vector described in the parent advisory also remains available.

**Distinction from the existing broadcast-pool advisory.** GHSA-mw8r-mw84-88v2 concerns the publish port, where an anonymous session is expected to connect and the defect is that broadcast content is not gated for it afterwards. This report concerns the kernel port with an access auth code configured, where the session should never be admitted in the first place. The leaked data overlaps because both end in the same broadcast pool, but the mechanisms and the affected deployments are different, and gating publish sessions does not close this path.

### Proof of Concept

Kernel port, `--accessAuthCode` set. Three WebSocket connections, none carrying credentials of any kind.

| Socket | Query | Result |
|---|---|---|
| A, baseline | `?app=siyuan&id=main&type=main` | Rejected, closed 1002, 0 frames |
| B, control | `?app=siyuan&id=auth&type=auth` | Connects, 0 frames |
| C, attack | `?app=siyuan&id=main&type=main&id=auth&type=auth` | Connects, 19 to 30 frames across two runs |

Socket A establishes that the access auth code is enforced. Socket B establishes that the existing quarantine works exactly as intended, admitting the keepalive session but delivering nothing to it. Socket C differs from B only in the duplicated parameters, and receives the event stream.

Frames observed on socket C included `savedoc` (`"action":"create","data":{"Root":{"ID": ...`), `transactions` (`"action":"updateAttrs"` carrying document titles), `filetreeSortChanged` (the notebook's complete ordered `childIDs`), `create` (a notebook object including its `name`), and `backgroundtask`.

A canary string placed inside a document body did not appear in any frame, on a full-text search of all captured frames.

### Impact

An unauthenticated remote caller obtains the kernel's live event stream on a deployment protected by an access auth code, with no user interaction and no prior knowledge of the instance.

Precisely what is disclosed: document identifiers and titles, notebook identifiers and names, file paths, the complete ordered child structure of notebooks, and the full stream of create, update and delete operations as they occur. Document body content is not present in the observed frames.

That set corresponds to the disclosure claimed by GHSA-xp2m-98x8-rpj6, which means the remediation for that advisory is bypassable rather than incomplete in scope. The absence of origin validation on the endpoint additionally preserves the cross-origin reachability described there.

Confidentiality only. No frames observed permitted writes.

### Suggested fix

Make both checks agree, and stop re-parsing attacker-controlled input after admission.

1. In the exemption, parse the query rather than matching substrings, and require `id` and `type` each to equal `auth` exactly.
2. Reject requests carrying duplicated query keys on this endpoint, so no URI can present two identities.
3. Record the exemption as a flag on the session at connect time, and have `IsAuthSession` read that flag rather than re-parsing the request. A session admitted under the keepalive exemption is then quarantined by construction, independent of how its URI is read later.

Adding origin validation to `/ws` would additionally close the cross-origin vector.

### Summary

`/api/filetree/authFilePublishAccess` is registered with `CheckAuth` only and is reachable anonymously. It never sets a failure code, so its outcome is signalled entirely by the response message and by whether a `Set-Cookie` header is present. Those two signals differ across access tiers, which lets an anonymous caller determine, for any candidate document identifier, whether that document is public or nonexistent, password-protected, or exists at the hidden or forbidden tier.

Separately, hidden and forbidden entries carry an empty password. Submitting `password:""` therefore satisfies the equality check for them, and the server responds by issuing `Set-Cookie: publish-auth-<docID>` for a document whose own tier is forbidden.

### Details

**Route,** identical on both refs:

```go
ginServer.Handle("POST", "/api/filetree/authFilePublishAccess", model.CheckAuth, authFilePublishAccess)
```

No `CheckAdminRole`, no `CheckReadonly`.

**Handler,** `kernel/api/filetree.go:1608` on the development branch and `:1421` on master. `ret.Code` is never assigned on the failure path, so every response carries `code:0`. The branch is:

```go
if item.Password == password {
    // SetPublishAuthCookie
} else {
    ret.Msg = Conf.Language(285)
}
```

**The cookie is issued for forbidden documents.** Entries at the hidden and forbidden tiers store `Password == ""`. A request with `password:""` therefore makes `item.Password == password` true for them, and the handler takes the success branch. The server issues a publish-auth cookie for a document it otherwise treats as inaccessible.

The cookie itself confers nothing, because those tiers are decided before any password check elsewhere in the codebase. The defect is that the endpoint's success signal does not correspond to access being granted, and that signal is observable.

**Three distinguishable outcomes.** With `password:""`, one request per candidate identifier:

| Tier of the target | `Set-Cookie` | Body |
|---|---|---|
| Public (no publish-access entry) | absent | `{"code":0,"msg":""}` |
| Nonexistent identifier | absent | `{"code":0,"msg":""}` |
| Password-protected | absent | `{"code":0,"msg":"Password is incorrect"}` |
| Hidden | **present** | `{"code":0,"msg":""}` |
| Forbidden | **present** | `{"code":0,"msg":""}` |

Public and nonexistent are indistinguishable from each other, which is correct. Everything else separates. A caller learns whether a given identifier names a password-protected document, or a document that exists at the hidden or forbidden tier, which is precisely the class the publish tiers exist to conceal.

**Identifiers are readily available.** Document and block identifiers appear in the DOM of published pages, in reference and backlink payloads, and in annotation reference data. The caller does not need to guess them.

**A fourth response on the development branch.** `IsEncryptedPublishRuntimeTarget` sets `ret.Code = -1`, which identifies the supplied identifier as belonging to an encrypted notebook. That is a membership oracle for encrypted notebooks, the same data class as `GHSA-f2rw-w22v-54vh`.

### Proof of Concept

Publish mode enabled, `Publish.Auth.Enable` false, anonymous client. One request per candidate identifier, all with an empty password:

```
POST /api/filetree/authFilePublishAccess
{"id":"<candidate document id>","password":""}
```

Comparing the response message and the presence of `Set-Cookie` against the table above classifies the identifier. Documents at the hidden and forbidden tiers return a publish-auth cookie and an empty message, distinguishing them both from public documents and from identifiers that name nothing at all.

### Impact

An anonymous reader in publish mode, or any publish `RoleReader`, can classify arbitrary document identifiers by access tier and confirm the existence of documents at the hidden and forbidden tiers. On the development branch the same endpoint additionally reveals whether an identifier belongs to an encrypted notebook.

Scoped precisely: no document content is disclosed and no privilege is gained, since the issued cookie is inert for these tiers. The value is as a confirmation primitive, turning an identifier obtained elsewhere into a definite statement about a document the reader is not permitted to see.

Confidentiality only, with no integrity or availability impact.

### Suggested fix

Return an identical response for every failure and for every tier the caller may not access, with no `Set-Cookie` header and no distinguishing message. In particular, do not treat an empty stored password as a successful match: hidden and forbidden entries should short-circuit before the password comparison rather than satisfying it. The encrypted-notebook branch should return the same generic response as everything else rather than its own code.

A rate limit on this endpoint would be a reasonable additional hardening measure, though it does not address the disclosure above.

### Summary

`/api/av/getAttributeViewBacklinks` filters its results for reader roles through `FilterAttributeViewBacklinksByPublishAccess`. That function resolves its ignore list with `GetDisablePublishAccess`, which covers only the forbidden tier. Documents at the hidden tier are absent from that list, so they pass the check.

The result is that an anonymous reader supplying a publicly visible database row receives the database name, row title and document path of rows in hidden documents that reference it.

The rest of the function is correct. It takes `*gin.Context` and calls `GetPathPasswordByPublishAccess` and `CheckPublishAuthCookie` at all four decision points, so the password-protected and private tiers are properly enforced. The defect is the choice of list, on one line.

### Details

**Route,** `kernel/api/router.go:545` on the development branch and `:527` on master:

```go
ginServer.Handle("POST", "/api/av/getAttributeViewBacklinks", model.CheckAuth, getAttributeViewBacklinks)
```

`CheckAuth` only. No `CheckAdminRole`, no `CheckReadonly`.

**The defect.** In `FilterAttributeViewBacklinksByPublishAccess` (`kernel/model/publish_access.go:1060` on dev, `:435` on master):

```go
publishIgnore := GetDisablePublishAccess(publishAccess)
```

`GetDisablePublishAccess` returns only entries at the forbidden tier. A hidden document has `visible:false`, `password:""`, `disable:false`, so it does not appear in that list. `CheckPathAccessableByPublishIgnore` therefore returns true for it, and because the password is empty the authentication branch short-circuits. Hidden documents pass both halves of the check.

**The sibling filter uses the correct list.** The regular backlink panel is the same product feature in the same UI, and it is gated properly. `kernel/api/ref.go:170` `getBacklink2` calls `FilterPathsByPublishAccess`, which at `kernel/model/publish_access.go:1256` resolves its list with `GetInvisiblePublishAccess`. Two backlink filters in the same file, opposite list choices.

**The distinction the tiers are meant to draw.** The shipped description of the hidden tier, from `app/appearance/langs/en.json`:

```
publishAccessHiddenComment = "Not publicly visible, can be accessed directly."
```

A direct-access endpoint using the forbidden list is consistent with that: hidden documents are meant to be reachable when the caller already knows the identifier. Backlink discovery is not direct access. The caller supplies the target row and receives the identities of referring rows it never named, which is enumeration, and enumeration is precisely what "not publicly visible" excludes.

**Origin.** The filter was introduced by `6da2c736e` (2026-07-18, "Show database relation backlinks in the attribute panel", #10599) with this list choice from the start. No security-focused commit has touched the attribute-view backlink path since.

**What is returned.** Per matched backlink: `AvName` (the database name), `Title` (the row title), `DatabasePath` (the HPath of the containing document), `BoxID`, `DatabaseBlockID`, and `Relations[].KeyName`. These are author-written names and titles, not opaque identifiers.

### Proof of Concept

Publish mode enabled, `Publish.Auth.Enable` false, anonymous client with no credentials or cookies. Document A is public and holds a database with a row. Document B is set to varying tiers and holds a database whose relation field points at A's row. The attacker needs only A's `avID` and `itemID`, both present in the DOM of A's own published page.

Listing control first, establishing that the platform agrees B must not be listed:

```
POST /api/filetree/listDocsByPath
→ returns only the public document
```

Then the same backlinks request at four tier settings, spaced to clear the 30-second `GetPublishAccess()` cache:

| Tier of document B | Result |
|---|---|
| Hidden (`visible:false`, no password, `disable:false`) | `total:1`, with `avName`, `title`, `databasePath` and `relations[].keyName` for the row in B |
| Forbidden (`disable:true`) | `total:0` |
| Private (password set) | `total:0` |
| Hidden again (restored) | `total:1`, reproducible |

The forbidden row confirms that the disable list is what the filter consults. The private row confirms that the password half works correctly. The gap is the hidden tier alone.

```
POST /api/av/getAttributeViewBacklinks
{"avID":"<public database id>","itemID":"<public row id>"}

→ 200, total:1, disclosing the database name, row title and document path
       of a document the same session cannot list
```

### Impact

An anonymous reader in publish mode, or any publish `RoleReader`, discovers that a hidden document contains a database row referencing a public one, and receives that row's title, its database's name, and the containing document's path. Names and titles are author-written and routinely describe their subject, so this discloses both the existence and the topic of documents the author marked as not publicly visible.

The reader does not need to know anything about the hidden document beforehand. The only input is a public row identifier taken from a page they are already entitled to view.

Confidentiality only, with no integrity or availability impact. No document body content is returned.

### Suggested fix

Change the list resolution in `FilterAttributeViewBacklinksByPublishAccess` to `GetInvisiblePublishAccess`, mirroring `FilterPathsByPublishAccess` on the regular backlink path. The password handling in the function is already correct and needs no change.

### Impact
The Streamable HTTP transport was constructed without `enableDnsRebindingProtection`/`allowedHosts`/`allowedOrigins` and performed no `Origin`-header validation. With the documented `auth.mode: "none"` loopback default, a **drive-by web page could `POST http://127.0.0.1/mcp`** and receive caller `http-local` with scopes `["*"]` — full vault read/write — via DNS rebinding / a forged Origin.

### Patches
Fixed in **1.3.1**. Upgrade to `>= 1.3.1`. The transport now enables DNS-rebinding protection and allowed hosts/origins and returns HTTP 403 on an invalid Origin (per MCP 2025-11-25).

### Workarounds
Do not expose the HTTP transport with `auth.mode: "none"`; require JWT auth, or bind to a non-loopback interface behind a proxy that validates `Origin`.

### Impact
Bridge tool results filtered only the `items` array against the read ACL and passed sibling fields through unfiltered: `tasks_filter` emitted `groups` whose counts reflected denied notes, `makemd_query` returned `...result` siblings, and `list_templates` enumerated Templater template paths and parsed user-function bodies with no read-whitelist gate. A caller could infer or read data from notes outside its read ACL.

### Patches
Fixed in **1.3.1**. Upgrade to `>= 1.3.1`. All path-attributable fields are now scrubbed or fail-closed, and `list_templates` is gated on the read whitelist.

### Workarounds
Disable the affected bridge tools (`tasks_filter`, `makemd_query`, `list_templates`) via tool visibility.

cwe.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

cves.summary:
### Summary
On a Streamable HTTP deployment with `auth.jwtSecret` configured, serving a 2026-07-28-era client that declared `elicitation.form` support, a call to a dispatch-gated tool (`destructive: true`, or a scope with an HITL floor) that was offered an `inputRequired` confirmation could still complete after the human declined, cancelled, or the elicitation response was omitted or malformed, provided the client echoed the validly bound `requestState` on resubmission. The server trusted an authentic, call-bound state as proof of approval; the state is minted before the elicitation leg is asked, so it proves only that the resubmission belongs to the same call.

### Details
Reproduced directly: a `destructive: true` tool call, offered `inputRequired`, answered with `{action: "decline"}` on the `elicitation/create` leg, still wrote. Present since the 2026-07-28 round trip shipped in v1.13.0 (THE-583). Only dispatch-gated tools were reachable; the sixteen handler-side conditionally gated tools (`write_note` overwrite, `move_note`, and others) did not read the elicitation state on the modern wire at all, so they neither let a decline nor an approval through.

### Impact
A client that echoes state after a decline can execute destructive vault operations (delete, cross-folder move, frontmatter replace, link rewrite) that the human explicitly refused. The precondition is a compliant client behaving incorrectly or a client under an attacker's control; the human's refusal is not enforced by the server.

### Patches
Fixed in 1.31.4: the server now also requires the confirm leg's own response (`inputResponse`) to be `{action: "accept", content: {approve: true}}` before trusting the echoed state. A declined, cancelled or not-approved round renders the ordinary `elicit_required` error and is never offered a second round for the same declined confirmation. The same release adds server-initiated in-band confirmation on stdio (legacy era), so stdio agents no longer need to mint `elicit_token` themselves.

### Not addressed
A malicious or non-compliant client can still answer its own `elicitation/create` leg with an approval regardless of what the human said. The server cannot verify that the client rendered the form or that a human saw it; this is inherent to the client-driven half of the 2026-07-28 protocol. The legacy shim, where the server sends and owns the leg, does not share this gap.

### Workarounds
Run affected deployments over stdio, or leave `auth.jwtSecret` unset so the `requestState` codec (and therefore `inputRequired`) is never offered; both fall back to the CLI `elicit_token` path.

### Credit
Reported in GH #967; found and closed under THE-1106 (PR #969); the residual is documented in SECURITY.md.

### References
- PR #969, GH #967, CHANGELOG `## [1.31.4] ### Security`
- `packages/server/src/mcp/server.ts` (`tools/call` handler), `packages/server/src/vault/hitl.ts`

### Impact
Tool dispatch did not check the caller-supplied `input.vault` against the caller's bound vault (`ctx.vaultId`); the folder ACL was a single global instance and the JWT carried no vault claim. As a result, **any valid token could read, write, or delete any configured vault** by passing `input.vault`, defeating multi-tenant isolation across ~90 tool sites. (`resources/read` was the only surface that already guarded this.)

### Patches
Fixed in **1.3.1** (the fix was developed on the `v1.3.0` tag, which never published to npm; 1.3.1 is the first published release with the fix). Upgrade to `>= 1.3.1`.

### Workarounds
Run a single vault per server process, or isolate each tenant on a separate process/credential.

### Fix
A central `input.vault === ctx.vaultId` guard was added in dispatch before the scope check.

### Impact
With a default configuration, an undefined `readPaths`/`writePaths` meant allow-all, the `strictReadDefault` flag was inert, and the `.obsidian`/`.git`/`.trash` control directories were denied only during enumeration — not on the direct request path. A caller could read `.obsidian/plugins/*/data.json`, exfiltrating **plugin API keys and Obsidian Sync passwords** (live-reproduced), as well as any other in-vault file by path.

### Patches
Fixed in **1.3.1**. Upgrade to `>= 1.3.1`. The default now denies `.obsidian`/`.git`/`.trash` on read/write/delete and honors `strictReadDefault` on the request path.

### Workarounds
Set an explicit `readPaths`/`writePaths` whitelist that excludes the control directories.

cwe.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

cves.summary:
### Impact
ACL checks ran on the lexical vault-relative path while containment used the realpath. An in-vault symlink placed under an allowed glob, whose realpath resolved into a denied folder, passed the read ACL — an intra-vault read-ACL-scope bypass. It requires an out-of-band-planted symlink (no MCP tool creates one) and is not a vault-root escape.

### Patches
Fixed in **1.3.1**. Upgrade to `>= 1.3.1`. ACL enforcement now derives the realpath vault-relative path and feeds a single unified predicate at every site.

### Workarounds
Do not permit untrusted symlinks inside the vault.

### Summary

A vulnerability in ZITADEL’s Login V2 UI allowed a password-verified browser session to be reused for a new authentication request without re-checking a user’s enrolled second factor (TOTP, OTP, or U2F). An attacker who already knows valid credentials can fully authenticate to an application without completing MFA.

### Impact

ZITADEL Login V2 issues a session as soon as the user’s password is verified, before the MFA challenge is completed. If the MFA step is abandoned (for example by navigating back) and login is started again, Login V2 may reuse that existing session instead of requiring the second factor.

Session validity checks only enforced MFA verification when the organization’s login policy had **Force MFA** (or **Force MFA for local users only**) enabled. They did not treat a voluntarily enrolled second factor as required. In the common case where MFA is available on the user but not organization-mandated, a password-only session was treated as fully authenticated and used to complete the OIDC or SAML callback, bypassing the user’s second factor.

**Scope note:** This issue affects **customer applications** that authenticate users through the hosted **Login V2** UI (OIDC/SAML). It does **not** affect Login V1. It also does **not** affect authentication to ZITADEL itself — including the Console, the Management/Admin APIs, and user self-management — even when Login V2 is enabled.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.0.0` through `4.16.0` (including RC versions)

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases. The patch ensures Login V2 validates that any second factor enrolled on the user has been verified before an existing session can be reused to complete authentication.

* **4.x**: Upgrade to $\ge$ [4.16.1](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/releases/tag/v4.16.1)

### Workarounds

If an immediate upgrade is not possible, enable **Force MFA** (or **Force MFA for local users only**, if you want to exempt IdP/federated logins) in the affected organization’s — or the instance default — login policy. This makes second-factor verification mandatory for password logins and closes this session-reuse bypass.

Note that this is a broader policy change (MFA becomes mandatory for the scoped local logins) rather than a narrow fix limited to users who already self-enrolled a second factor.

### Questions

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please email us at [security@zitadel.com](mailto:security@zitadel.com)

### Credits

Thanks to Philippe Wechsler ([@MadMonkey87](https://github.com/MadMonkey87)) for finding and reporting the vulnerability.

### Summary

A vulnerability in ZITADEL Actions V1 allows an organization Action author to read files from the ZITADEL host filesystem through the JavaScript `require()` module loader. On common self-hosted deployments this can be chained to steal bootstrap credentials (including the Login Client PAT) and escalate from a single-tenant organization owner to instance administrator.

### Impact

ZITADEL Actions V1 run custom JavaScript inside the ZITADEL server process at OIDC, SAML, and login-flow trigger points. The runtime enables the goja Node-compatible `require()` registry without restricting the source loader, so Action scripts can load host files readable by the ZITADEL process (notably `.js` and `.json`, and in some cases other file contents via error channels).

An attacker with **ORG_OWNER** on any organization (which includes `org.action.write` and `org.flow.write`) can therefore:

* Read process-readable host files, including configuration or secrets mounted into the API container (for example service-account material, projected secrets, or config carrying sensitive values).
* On deployments that follow ZITADEL’s documented bootstrap paths (`ZITADEL_FIRSTINSTANCE_LOGINCLIENTPATPATH`, `ZITADEL_FIRSTINSTANCE_MACHINEKEYPATH`), recover instance-wide credentials such as the **IAM_LOGIN_CLIENT** PAT or the **IAM_OWNER** service-account key, enabling escalation to full instance control.

This collapses the expected multi-tenant isolation boundary: a tenant organization administrator is not meant to access host filesystem secrets or instance-wide credentials.

**Scope note:** This issue affects **Actions V1**. Host command execution was not identified as part of this vulnerability. Impact depends on what the ZITADEL process can read on disk and on deployment layout — documented Compose and quick-start setups that write bootstrap PATs or machine keys into the API container amplify severity.

### Affected Versions

Systems running one of the following versions are affected:

* **4.x:** `4.0.0` through `4.16.0` (including RC versions)
* **3.x:** `3.0.0` through `3.4.12` (including RC versions)

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed in the latest releases. The patch disables filesystem-backed module loading for Action scripts so that only the intended native `zitadel/*` modules can be required.

* **4.x**: Upgrade to $\ge$ [4.16.1](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/releases/tag/v4.16.1)
* **3.x**: Upgrade to $\ge$ [3.4.13](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel/releases/tag/v3.4.13)

### Workarounds

If an immediate upgrade is not possible:

* Restrict who can create, update, or attach Actions — do not grant `org.action.write` / `org.flow.write` (or **ORG_OWNER**) to untrusted administrators in multi-tenant environments.
* Audit existing Actions for `require()` of filesystem paths.
* Remove or relocate bootstrap credential files (`login-client.pat`, machine keys) so they are not readable inside the API process filesystem.
* Limit host filesystem exposure for the ZITADEL process (no unnecessary readable secrets beside the binary).

### Questions

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please email us at [security@zitadel.com](mailto:security@zitadel.com)

### Credits

Thanks to Dor Konis ([@dkonis](https://github.com/dkonis)) and Feras Daragma ([@FerasTr](https://github.com/FerasTr)) from GE Vernova, and to [pyuysig](https://github.com/pyuysig), for finding and reporting this vulnerability.
